title: Threat model RBAC v2: privilege escalation + impersonation risks and mitigations
creator: Marcus Lin
description:
Goal
Threat model the RBAC v2 authorization path and admin workflows with focus on:
- Privilege escalation paths (including role assignment, policy distribution/versioning, cached decisions)
- Support impersonation / break-glass risks
- Required mitigations and concrete engineering work items (library, services, console, audit logs)

In-scope surfaces
- Control plane APIs + gateway/middleware checks (RBAC v2 dual-eval and enforcement modes)
- Console backend routes for admin/security settings
- Role assignment + SSO/SAML group mapping flows
- Break-glass + support impersonation (time-bounded elevated sessions)
- Policy bundle distribution (Hosted/Dedicated/Private, incl. air-gapped) and policy cache invalidation
- Audit logging enrichment for authz decisions

Out of scope
- Data-plane inference request authorization beyond org/project scoping
- Identity provider deep refactors beyond claim->role mapping validation

Artifacts / references
- Confluence: RBAC v2 overview (sources/confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/rbac-v2-overview.json)
- Confluence: Authz check standard (sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/authz-check-standard.json)
- ADR: Policy format + evaluation semantics (sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-014-rbac-v2-policy-format.json)
- Confluence: Authz decision audit logging spec (sources/confluence/security-and-compliance/audit-logging/authz-decision-audit-logging.json)
- Internal: Support break-glass runbook (sources/confluence/policies-and-process/access-and-permissions/support-break-glass-access.json)

Attendees (live session)
- Jordan Lee (policy engine)
- Kaitlyn Nguyen (authz implementation)
- Chloe Martin (console backend)
- Amara Diallo (gateway)
- Kevin Osei (audit logging)
- Sean Gallagher + Rafael Mendes (SRE workflows)
- Marcus Lin (security)

System model (condensed)
Assets
- Role assignments (org + project scope)
- Policy bundles (versioned, signed for Private)
- Authorization decisions (allow/deny + reason codes)
- Audit log events and SIEM exports
- Support elevated session grants / impersonation session tokens

Trust boundaries
- User browser <-> Console backend
- Client <-> API Gateway <-> Control plane services
- Support tooling (admin) <-> control plane
- Policy bundle distribution channel (Hosted/CDN; Private installer/update)

Primary actors
- Customer Org Admin / Security Admin / Billing Admin / Developer / Read-only
- Support engineer (with/without elevated session)
- SRE on-call (break-glass)
- Automation (CI/CD, installer/upgrader)

Threat model findings
1) Privilege escalation via role assignment endpoints
Risk: attacker with limited access gains ability to grant roles to self/others (org admin, security admin) or grant project-wide roles.
Vectors:
- Missing/partial checks on role assignment endpoints or console routes
- Confused deputy: backend service uses service credentials and trusts caller-supplied org_id / principal_id
- IDOR: role assignment APIs accept principal IDs not bound to org membership
Mitigations (required):
- Enforce RBAC v2 permission on ALL role assignment operations: create/update/delete role assignment and SSO group mapping changes.
- Validate subject invariants server-side: principal must be member of org; mapping changes require Security Admin.
- Add service-side authorization context: derive org/project scope from authn context, not request body.
- Explicitly block self-escalation patterns: if actor is modifying own role, require higher permission (or disallow unless Org Admin) and log as high-risk.
Engineering actions:
- Add dedicated permission names for: org.role_assignments.manage, org.sso_mappings.manage.
- Add integration tests: Developer cannot grant roles; Billing Admin cannot modify SSO mapping.

2) Privilege escalation via policy bundle tampering / downgrade
Risk: policy bundle replaced or downgraded to a permissive version; private deployments accept unsigned policies or stale versions.
Vectors:
- Unsigned policy bundle distribution for Private
- Bundle version skew between console and control plane (evaluation differences)
- Downgrade attacks if version checks are absent
Mitigations (required):
- Private: policy bundles must be signed; installer/upgrader verifies signature and enforces monotonic version unless explicit break-glass override.
- Hosted/Dedicated: pin minimum policy schema version in services; reject incompatible bundles; emit audit event on bundle update.
- Add policy provenance to audit logs: policy_version + bundle_hash.
Engineering actions:
- Policy bundle verifier library function: Verify(bundle) -> {version, hash, signer}.
- Audit event: policy_bundle.updated with actor + source (automation vs admin) + hash.

3) Impersonation abuse (support impersonation and session fixation)
Risk: support engineer or attacker obtains ability to impersonate customer users, leading to unauthorized actions, data access, or configuration changes.
Vectors:
- Impersonation endpoint too broad; no explicit approval
- Impersonation tokens long-lived; not bound to ticket/approval
- Weak auditability: actions attributed only to impersonated user
Mitigations (required):
- Support impersonation MUST require time-bounded elevated session grant (break-glass style) with explicit reason + ticket ID.
- Impersonation session should be separate principal type; actions must log both: actor (support) and subject (impersonated).
- Hard scope limits: only for specific org/project; no cross-org browsing; disallow billing operations under impersonation unless explicitly granted.
- UI + API must show banner/flag when in impersonation mode.
Engineering actions:
- Standardize audit fields: actor_type=support, actor_id, elevated_session_id, impersonated_user_id.
- Add reason code for denials involving impersonation restrictions (403 SUPPORT_IMPERSONATION_DISALLOWED_FOR_ACTION).

4) Break-glass escalation without sufficient controls
Risk: elevated session grant becomes a backdoor (too easy to obtain, too broad, too long-lived).
Vectors:
- Single-approver flow
- No alerting on usage
- Elevated session not revocable or not enforced consistently across services
Mitigations (required):
- 2-person approval for production orgs (Support Lead/SRE Lead + Security on-call) except declared incidents (documented exception).
- Short TTL (<= 60 minutes) with explicit scope (org + permission set) and immediate revocation capability.
- Mandatory alerting: Slack + PagerDuty when created/used for P0 actions.
- Enforce via shared middleware: elevated_session must be checked in authz library.
Engineering actions:
- Add dedicated audit events: elevated_session.granted / elevated_session.used / elevated_session.revoked.
- Metrics + alerts: count of elevated sessions, usage by action, after-hours usage.

5) Cache invalidation / stale authorization decisions
Risk: user removed from role retains access due to cached policy/role data.
Vectors:
- Per-org cache not invalidated on role assignment updates
- Multi-region propagation delays
Mitigations (required):
- Invalidate caches on any role assignment or membership change (best-effort + periodic revalidation).
- Add max-staleness bound (e.g., hard TTL) and include cache_age in logs/metrics.
Engineering actions:
- Emit role_assignment.changed event to cache invalidation bus.
- Dashboard: authz_cache_hit_rate, authz_cache_staleness_p95, shadow_denies_by_cache_age.

6) Confused deputy between gateway and services (double evaluation mismatches)
Risk: gateway allows but service denies (or vice versa) due to mismatched policy versions, scope derivation, or incomplete enforcement.
Vectors:
- Partial enforcement: some services rely on gateway, others do local checks
- Shadow mode confusion: operators believe enforcement exists when it is only metric collection
Mitigations (required):
- Establish enforcement rule: services must enforce locally for any state-changing action; gateway may pre-check for UX but is not the source of truth.
- Include evaluated_at + policy_version in both gateway and service logs to debug mismatches.
Engineering actions:
- Update authz-check standard docs to clarify (if not already explicit).
- Add conformance test: state-changing endpoints require service-side check.

7) Audit log integrity / attribution gaps
Risk: inability to prove who did what; attackers attempt to hide actions by exploiting missing logging or ambiguous actor.
Vectors:
- Missing allow/deny decision logs for sensitive operations
- Logs missing reason codes/policy version
Mitigations (required):
- For sensitive actions (P0/P1), emit authz decision context (allow/deny) and actor/role/policy version in audit logs.
- Deny events: record attempted action + resource scope.
Engineering actions:
- Implement structured logging fields across services and exporter mapping validation.

Risk ranking (summary)
- High: impersonation misuse; break-glass backdoor; role assignment escalation; policy bundle tampering
- Medium: cache staleness; gateway/service mismatch; audit attribution gaps

Decisions
- Deny-overrides semantics are required to support explicit deny constraints for impersonation/break-glass limitations (align with ADR-014).
- Impersonation will be treated as a first-class principal mode; never silently “become the user” without dual attribution.

Deliverables from this ticket
- Threat model notes (this description) + prioritized mitigations
- Concrete follow-up engineering issues (see below)

Follow-up tasks (created)
- ENG-5412: Add explicit permissions + tests for role assignment + SSO mapping endpoints
- ENG-5413: Impersonation restrictions + dual-attribution audit fields in authz library and console
- ENG-5414: Policy bundle signing verification + downgrade protection for Private
- ENG-5415: Cache invalidation on role assignment changes + staleness metrics
- ENG-5416: Add high-signal alerts for elevated session grants/usage

Acceptance criteria
- Security sign-off from Marcus Lin that impersonation + break-glass mitigations meet minimum bar for enterprise evaluation
- Audit logging spec includes fields for elevated_session_id and impersonated_user_id and is implementable across Hosted/Dedicated/Private
- Actionable follow-up issues exist with owners and clear scope
comments: 2025-02-11 (Marcus Lin): Creating this as the dedicated threat model task. We’ve had multiple questions from enterprise prospects on separation of duties + support access; we need crisp mitigations before we flip enforcement broadly.

2025-02-14 (Jordan Lee): Scheduled 90-min working session with Kaitlyn/Chloe/Amara/Kevin + SRE. Focus: impersonation + break-glass + policy distribution threats. Will publish notes back here and open follow-ups.

2025-02-18 (Sean Gallagher): Please include incident-time reality: on-call needs to change routing/fallback + view org config quickly. Break-glass flow can’t be too heavy, but must be auditable and time-bounded.

2025-02-20 (Kevin Osei): For audit evidence, we need deny events too (attempted sensitive actions), and we need to export actor + role_ids + policy_version to SIEM. Make sure impersonation attributes both support actor and customer subject.

2025-02-24 (Kaitlyn Nguyen): One risk: self-role-change endpoints. We should explicitly block or require higher permission to avoid ‘Developer grants self Org Admin’ if any gap exists. I’ll add integration tests once permission names are finalized.

2025-02-26 (Jordan Lee): Drafted the threat model summary + opened follow-up ENG-5412..ENG-5416 with owners. Main decision: treat impersonation as principal mode w/ explicit deny constraints; audit must include elevated_session_id and impersonated_user_id.

2025-03-03 (Marcus Lin): Reviewed. Looks good. Biggest remaining concern is downgrade protection for Private policy bundles; Hanae asked for monotonic version enforcement and explicit override path. Marking this Done once ENG-5414 is in progress.
2025-03-06 (Jordan Lee): ENG-5414 is created and assigned. Closing this ticket; ongoing work tracked in follow-ups.
